title: Bodhi Day
hookLine: some Buddhists keep the Buddha's awakening in December: the night under the tree, and the hand that touched the earth
tomorrow: why do the Hanukkah lights go up each night, not down?

lines: WHO DO YOU THINK YOU ARE?
A MAN SITS UNDER A FIG TREE.
cards: Some doubts arrive in a voice that sounds a lot like your own: who do you think you are? A man once sat under a fig tree with that question coming at him from every side.
He had left a palace, starved himself nearly to death, then given that up too. Now he sat down and vowed not to get up until he was free.
The stories say Mara came, the tempter, with storms and armies and his own daughters. Nothing moved him. So Mara tried a last question.
This seat isn't yours. Who will vouch for you?

teach.b: Siddhartha didn't argue. He drew his right hand out from his robe and reached it down to the earth.
And the old telling says the earth answered, with a roar: it was his witness. Mara's armies fled. Through the night his mind grew clear, and by dawn, tradition says, he had woken up.
That's what Buddha is: a title, the awakened one. The fig became the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. Here's what Buddhists do because of that night.
Look at a Buddha statue with the right hand hanging over the knee, fingertips touching the ground. That's this moment, the earth-touching gesture.
And some Buddhists, especially in Japan and in Zen communities, keep the night as Bodhi Day in December; in Japanese it's called Rohatsu.
Some Zen monasteries hold a hard stretch of sitting leading up to it, as if to keep the night with him. The teaching under the story is the Buddhist claim itself: a human being can wake up.
Not handed down by a god, not inherited by birth. In the old telling, the earth vouches for the long road behind him, his giving across many lives.
But the waking itself happens here, on ordinary ground, in one night of sitting. And look at how he met the doubt. No speech about his worth.
Just his hand on the ground he was already sitting on, and staying.

how: On Bodhi Day some Buddhists, especially in Japan and Zen communities (Rohatsu), sit long meditation, chant and remember the awakening; temples display the Buddha in the earth-touching gesture.

o: the Buddha's birthday, kept with gifts and a shared family meal
the day some Buddhists remember the Buddha waking up under the tree
a day for planting a new tree in memory of a teacher who died

games.q: the night under the tree: tap the pairs.
p: the tempter who asks who vouches for him
reaches down to touch the earth
the Zen name for the day

s: the hand touching the ground on Buddha statues remembers the night of the awakening
it's the earth-touching gesture: Siddhartha calling the earth as his witness against Mara.
Buddha is his personal name, like Siddhartha
it's a title: the awakened one.
Mara gave up after Siddhartha argued that he deserved the seat
he didn't argue. He touched the earth, and the earth answered.

games.q: a coworker says awakening is something a god hands down to a chosen few. what does the Bodhi tree story say?
o: no god hands it down: he touched the earth, sat through the night and woke up.
Mara gave up the seat once Siddhartha won the argument about who deserved it.
a god looked down, chose him, and woke him up from above.
games.why: In the story no god grants it. The earth witnesses to his long road of giving, and Siddhartha sits through the night and wakes up. That's the Buddhist claim: awakening is possible for a human being.

practice: Sit near a tree if you can, or picture one, wide and rooted. Rest your right hand on the floor or the ground beside you, fingertips down. Let the ground hold your weight for the whole sit.
If a thought comes asking who you think you are, don't answer it. Leave your hand where it is.

wordCard.voice: Bodhi Day: from bodhi, awakening. The day some Buddhists keep for the night Siddhartha woke up under the tree, with the earth as his witness.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening. The Bodhi tree is the tree of awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: awakening. He answered the doubt with one hand on the earth. Day 1639, under the tree.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka), the Bodhi tree: Mara claims the seat, the Bodhisatta stretches his right hand to the earth, the earth answers as witness; awakening by dawn
Asvaghosa, Buddhacarita 13-14 (Mara's assault; the awakening through the night)
Bodhi Day in living practice: Rohatsu in Japanese and Zen communities in December, with a week of intensive sitting (sesshin) in some monasteries; statues in the earth-touching gesture
